power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Malignant remodeling alters tissue mechanics, but biomechanical differences among primary head and neck tumors, benign cervical lymph nodes, and nodal metastases remain poorly characterized.

We used in vivo and ex vivo ultrasound shear-wave elastography (USE) and ex vivo tabletop MR elastography (ttMRE) to compare stiffness, viscoelasticity, and spatial heterogeneity across these tissue groups and to assess cross-modal agreement.
As a secondary objective, we explored whether primary-tumor biomechanics differed by pathological nodal status.
Methods: Eighteen patients -17 with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) and one with salivary duct carcinoma -underwent surgical resection.
Target cervical lymph nodes were assessed by in vivo USE, and resected lymph nodes and primary tumors by ex vivo USE.

Multifrequency ttMRE was successfully performed in 8 benign lymph nodes, 8 metastatic lymph nodes, and 13 primary tumors and yielded shear modulus μ, power-law exponent α, and spatial heterogeneity metrics.
Quantitative T1, T2, fat-fraction, and apparent-diffusioncoefficient (ADC) measurements were also performed.
Group comparisons used Kruskal-Wallis tests with Dunn-.
Tumor biomechanics emerge from interactions among malignant cells, extracellular matrix, vasculature, and interstitial fluid.

Matrix deposition, cross-linking, and fiber alignment can increase bulk tissue stiffness, while malignant cells within the same tumor may remain mechanically soft and motile; the measured phenotype therefore depends on spatial scale, loading, and imaging method [1] [2] [3] [4].

text.text: In head and neck malignancies, cervical nodal status is central to staging and treatment planning.

Although crosssectional imaging with CT, MRI, or FDG-PET/CT is mandatory to assess the size and local extent of the primary tumor as well as the presence of distant metastases, additional cervical ultrasonography is recommended for the assessment of cervical lymph nodes because of its higher diagnostic performance [7] [8] [9].

text.text: Nevertheless, nodal evaluation continues to rely substantially on size and morphological criteria.
USE adds a quantitative mechanical readout.

Tabletop MRE (ttMRE) enables high-frequency, high-resolution measurements in small excised specimens under controlled experimental conditions [39] [40] [41] [42].

text.text: In this prospective study, we combined in vivo and ex vivo USE with ex vivo ttMRE and quantitative T1, T2, fatfraction, and ADC mapping.

The primary objectives were to compare biomechanical parameters among benign cervical lymph nodes, metastatic cervical lymph nodes, and primary tumors and to assess agreement between ttMRE stiffness and USE shear-wave speed.

Secondary, exploratory objectives were to evaluate whether primarytumor biomechanics differed by pathological nodal status and to describe associations with quantitative MRI and qualitative histopathology.
>Materials and Methods

text.text: Eighteen patients with histopathologically confirmed head and neck malignancies who were scheduled for surgical resection were prospectively enrolled (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Eighteen patients with histopathologically confirmed head and neck malignancies who were scheduled for surgical resection were prospectively enrolled (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: One day before surgery, the operating surgeon performed in vivo USE of the target cervical lymph node and subsequently identified and retrieved the same node during neck dissection.

According to the study protocol, all resected target lymph nodes and primary-tumor specimens were scheduled for immediate ex vivo USE and ttMRE; when tissue volume was limited, diagnostic histopathology took priority.
Final histopathology confirmed head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) in 17 patients and salivary duct carcinoma in one.

The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee of Charité-Universitätsmedizin Berlin (protocol code EA4/214/23; date of approval: November 27, 2024), and written informed consent was obtained from all participants according to the Declaration of Helsinki.

All ultrasound examinations followed a standardized protocol using an Aplio i900 system (Canon Medical Systems Corporation, Tochigi, Japan) with a 4-10 MHz multifrequency linear-array transducer (center frequency, 7 MHz) [13, 14].
text.formatted: All ultrasound examinations followed a standardized protocol using an Aplio i900 system (Canon Medical Systems Corporation, Tochigi, Japan) with a 4-10 MHz multifrequency linear-array transducer (center frequency, 7 MHz) <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14]</ref>.

text.text: Patients were examined supine with the head extended and rotated contralaterally.
B-mode ultrasound was used to document target-node location, morphology, and short-and long-axis diameters.
USE based on acoustic radiation force impulse imaging was then performed in vivo.
Localized acoustic push pulses generated shear waves within the target node, and three consecutive two-dimensional acquisitions were obtained with the node centered in the field of view.
A circular region of interest (ROI) was manually placed within the node, and its size was adapted to the lesion.
Shear-wave speed (SWS, m/s) maps were generated, and the mean SWS and corresponding standard deviation across the three acquisitions were recorded.
Dual-image display of the B-mode image and color-coded USE map was used to verify lesion coverage.
Penetration depth was adapted to the individual node, whereas gain settings were held constant.
SWS was reported directly in m/s rather than converted to Young's modulus.
The commonly used conversion is 3 , (1) where E is Young's modulus, ρ is tissue density, and c is the SWS.

These assumptions are not generally valid in structurally heterogeneous cervical lymph nodes; direct reporting of SWS therefore avoids model-dependent inaccuracies [13, 14].

text.text: All in vivo examinations were performed one day before surgery by the surgeon who subsequently performed the tumor resection and neck dissection, facilitating reliable intraoperative identification of the target node.

The examiner held German Society for Ultrasound in Medicine (DEGUM) Level II certification, corresponding approximately to European Federation of Societies for Ultrasound in Medicine and Biology (EFSUMB) Level 2 competency in head and neck ultrasound [47].

text.text: Immediately after resection, the target lymph node and primary-tumor specimens underwent ex vivo USE using the same ARFI-based protocol.
Each resected specimen was examined once.
Mean SWS within a manually defined ROI was recorded as the ex vivo USE stiffness readout.

Tabletop MR elastography: setup and acquisition ttMRE was performed on a benchtop 0.5-T MRI system (Magspec, Pure Devices GmbH, Würzburg, Germany) equipped with a four-channel gradient amplifier (DC-600, Pure Devices GmbH) and a piezoelectric actuator (PAHL60/20, Piezosystem Jena GmbH).
The actuator generated vibrations along the longitudinal tube axis (Fig. 1C).
text.formatted: The actuator generated vibrations along the longitudinal tube axis (Fig. <ref type="figure">1C</ref>).

text.text: Fresh specimens were placed in cylindrical glass tubes with a 7-mm inner diameter and mechanically coupled using a PVC-foam spacer.

A spin-echo sequence with bipolar motion-encoding gradients directed along z encoded one 3-mm axial slice at 0.15 × 0.15 mm² in-plane resolution (64 × 64 matrix) at four phase offsets per vibration period.

The actuator was driven from 800 to 5000 Hz; 800 Hz yielded no evaluable wave field in any specimen, so retained frequencies spanned 900 to 5000 Hz, and in most specimens the retained range was 900-3300 Hz (Supplementary Table S1).

text.text: Echo time, repetition time, and motion-encoding-gradient amplitude were adjusted specimen-wise according to relaxation behavior.
This subsection describes acquisition only; processing is detailed below.
The hardware and acquisition principles follow Zhao et al. [41].

text.text: The complex wave field at each drive frequency was obtained after phase unwrapping and temporal Fourier transformation.
First, a global Bessel-function fit to the complex radial wave profile provided a specimen-level complex wavenumber and a prior for spatial filtering (Fig. 3).

text.text: Directional bandpass filtering then isolated quasiplane shear-wave components along eight directions.

From the spatial phase and amplitude gradients of the filtered complex fields, frequency-resolved maps of SWS(f) and penetration rate PR(f), both in m/s, were reconstructed pixel-wise [41, [48] [49] [50].

text.text: In contrast to frequency-and amplitude-weighted averaged maps described for other applications of this framework, no frequency-averaged SWS or PR maps were used here.

Instead, the frequency-resolved SWS(f) and PR(f) values at each pixel were fitted directly with a fractional spring-pot model to obtain shear modulus μ (reported in kPa; hereafter also referred to as stiffness) and power-law exponent α (dimensionless; α → 0 indicates more elastic and α → 1 more viscous behavior).

text.text: Quantitative analysis was restricted to the central 5.6-mm region of the 7-mm tube to reduce boundary effects.

Frequencies were retained only when the central analysis region showed adequate wave amplitude and phase signal-to-noise ratio and the wavelength was sufficiently sampled; frequencies were excluded when attenuation reduced the wave amplitude to the noise floor before the wave reached the analysis region or when the wavelength could not be resolved reliably [41].

text.text: Spatially isolated fitting failures in μ and α were corrected using an iterative log-space local-median filter.

A pixel was classified as a fitting failure when, after log10 transformation of the parameter map, it deviated from the median of its 5 × 5 neighborhood by more than four robust standard deviations (1.4826 × median absolute deviation, with a lower bound of 0.05 log10 units) and simultaneously differed from that local median by more than a factor of 20; pixels deviating from the specimenwide median by more than five robust standard deviations and meeting the same factor-20 criterion were also flagged.
At least eight valid neighboring pixels were required for a pixel to be evaluated.

Flagged pixels were replaced by the geometric median of the surrounding non-flagged pixels, with the window expanded from 5 × 5 to at most 21 × 21 until this minimum was reached, and the procedure was repeated for up to four iterations or until no further pixels were flagged.

Because a statistical and a ratio criterion had to be met simultaneously, only isolated implausible values were replaced and spatially coherent heterogeneity was preserved; the proportion of corrected pixels was recorded for each specimen.
Spatial heterogeneity (texture) was quantified for μ and α using the within-specimen standard deviation (SD), interquartile range (IQR), and Shannon entropy [5, 41].

text.text: Alcian blue was used to visualize glycosaminoglycan (GAG) accumulation and Sirius red to visualize collagen deposition and the apparent thickness of collagen fiber bundles.

For illustrative purposes, colorcoded fiber-orientation overlays of the Sirius red sections were generated with the OrientationJ plugin for ImageJ; these overlays served to display the predominant fiber direction and the visual degree of fiber alignment and were not used to compute orientation statistics.
MMP-9 immunostaining was inspected as a marker associated with extracellular-matrix degradation and remodeling.
Histological observations were evaluated descriptively.
2.8 Statistical analysis Analyses were conducted at the specimen level except for matched comparisons.
Continuous data are reported as median [IQR].
Three-group comparisons used Kruskal-Wallis tests followed, when significant, by Dunn tests with Bonferroni correction for three pairwise contrasts.
In vivo USE and primary-tumor comparisons by nodal status used two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests; matched specimens used two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves summarized metastatic-versus-benign node discrimination and, secondarily, nodal-status discrimination from primary tumors.
Area under the curve (AUC) confidence intervals were estimated by 2000-resample stratified bootstrap, and Youden thresholds were calculated in the study cohort.
AUCs were not formally compared.
Cross-modal associations were analyzed by Spearman correlation.

To account for repeated specimens from individual patients, tissue-class comparisons were repeated using linear mixed-effects models with tissue class as a fixed effect and patient as a random intercept.

The μ, SWS, μ-based dispersion, and joint metrics were log10-transformed for these models; omnibus effects were assessed by likelihood-ratio tests and pairwise contrasts by Bonferroni-corrected Wald tests.
Patient-level cluster bootstrapping (2000 resamples) provided additional AUC and correlation confidence intervals.
The nominal threshold was two-sided p < 0.05.
text.formatted: The nominal threshold was two-sided p < 0.05.

text.text: Across 11 ttMRE tissue-class omnibus tests, Bonferroni-adjusted sensitivity analyses confirmed all 7 nominally significant findings (adjusted p = 0.002-0.027).
Primary-tumor nodal-status and biomechanical-MRI association analyses were exploratory; the prespecified ttMRE μ-USE SWS correlation was assessed separately.

text.text: All 18 patients underwent in vivo USE before surgery.

Ex vivo USE was available for 9 benign lymph nodes, 11 metastatic lymph nodes, and all 18 primary tumors (Fig. 1, Table 2). ttMRE was evaluable in 8 benign lymph nodes, 8 metastatic lymph nodes, and 13 primary tumors (7 node-negative, N-, and 6 node-positive, N+; Fig. 1, Table 1). ttMRE exclusions resulted from insufficient specimen dimensions (smaller than the glass tube diameter, 7 mm), inadequate wave-field quality, prioritization of tissue for diagnostic histopathology, or inability to complete the time-intensive measurement workflow.

text.text: Of the 18 tumors initially diagnosed as HNSCC, one was reclassified as salivary duct carcinoma on final surgical histopathology.
The salivary duct carcinoma showed biomechanical values within the range observed among the HNSCC tumors and was retained in the analysis; its exclusion did not alter the group-level conclusions.

Using in vivo and ex vivo USE together with spatially resolved multifrequency ttMRE, we characterized primary head and neck tumors and their corresponding cervical lymph nodes within the same patients.

The principal finding was a consistent benign-versus-metastatic nodal stiffness contrast that was reproduced across all three acquisition settings and supported by positive cross-modal rank correlations. ttMRE additionally resolved stiffness-related spatial heterogeneity, although most heterogeneity measures remained strongly coupled to μ and therefore describe the same underlying contrast rather than an independent one.

In a secondary analysis, primary tumors from node-positive patients had lower ttMRE μ than those from node-negative patients (uncorrected p = 0.035) -an exploratory association that was not reproduced by ex vivo USE and that points to a scale-and modality-dependent aspect of the tumor-node relationship.
Benign lymph nodes were consistently softer than metastatic nodes, in agreement with prior pathologyreferenced cervical-node USE studies and with MRE-based nodal work [11, 12, 37, 38].

text.text: That this contrast persisted across in vivo USE, ex vivo USE, and ttMRE is notable, because these three settings differ substantially in excitation frequency, mechanical boundary conditions, and the physical quantity reported.
A contrast that survives such differences is unlikely to be an artifact of any single acquisition geometry and more plausibly reflects a genuine difference in tissue composition.
Among the heterogeneity metrics, H(μ) is less directly scaledependent than SD(μ) and IQR(μ), since entropy responds to the shape of the parameter distribution rather than its absolute level.
All three nevertheless remained closely related to μ and should be read as complementary descriptions of the same stiffness contrast rather than as independent confirmation of it [5].

Pairing removes between-patient baseline variation and can therefore expose consistent within-patient differences that remain hidden when unpaired group distributions overlap, as they did here.
This interpretation has clear limits.

The two paired comparisons involve different patient groups and cross-sectional specimens obtained at a single operation; they do not follow one lesion over time and consequently cannot demonstrate progressive mechanical amplification along a metastatic cascade.

What they do support is a patient-specific mechanical context, in which the relevant quantity may be the stiffness difference between a patient's own tissues rather than an absolute threshold applied across patients.
Longitudinal designs and larger matched cohorts would be required to distinguish these possibilities.
Primary tumors from node-positive patients had lower stiffness by ttMRE than tumors from node-negative patients (uncorrected p = 0.035).
Its interpretation depends critically on the scale of observation.

Bulk tissue stiffness integrates extracellular matrix composition, cellularity, necrosis, fluid content, and measurement conditions, and is not equivalent to the stiffness of the individual cancer cells embedded within it.
Mechanically soft or unjammed cancer-cell populations can coexist within an overall rigid tumor, and increased nuclear deformability has been shown to support invasion in HNSCC models [3, 52, 53].
